hints: Focus on what addition polymerisation tells you about mass, the repeat unit has exactly the same mass as the monomer.
Divide the total polymer $M_r$ by the number of repeat units to get the $M_r$ of one monomer, then work out the $M_r$ of each alkene option.
For the monomers that match that mass, draw the $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CHR-}$ backbone and check if the CH carbon has four different groups attached.
walkthrough:
**Find the mass of one repeat unit**

Think of the polymer as 2000 identical building blocks joined together. So one block must weigh the total divided by 2000.

$$M_r \text{ of repeat unit} = \frac{112000}{2000} = 56$$

**Link repeat unit to monomer**

In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bond just opens to single bonds. No atoms are lost, so $M_r$ of monomer = $M_r$ of repeat unit = 56.

Now check the options: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_3$ is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6 = 42$, $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3)_2$ is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8 = 56$, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8 = 56$, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} = 70$. Only two candidates have $M_r = 56$.

**Use the chiral centre clue**

A chiral carbon needs four different groups. Draw the polymer backbone.

For $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3)_2$ the polymer is $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-C(CH}_3)_2\text{]-}_n$. The substituted carbon has two identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so it can never be chiral.

For $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ the polymer is $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)]-}_n$. Each CH is joined to H, to $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and to two different chain continuations left and right, so it is a chiral centre. This fits both conditions.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_3$ is propene, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$ with $M_r = 42$. 2000 units would give $2000 \times 42 = 84000$, not 112000. Although its polymer $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)]-}$ would have chiral centres, the mass is wrong.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3)_2$ is 2-methylpropene, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ with $M_r = 56$, so the mass fits. However its polymer is $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-C(CH}_3)_2\text{]-}$. The substituted carbon carries two identical methyl groups, so it has only three distinct groups and is not chiral.
options.C: Correct. $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is but-1-ene, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ with $M_r = 56$. This gives $2000 \times 56 = 112000$ as required. Its polymer $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)]-}$ has a CH carbon bonded to H, ethyl, and two different polymer chain segments, making it a chiral centre.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ is pent-1-ene, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ with $M_r = 70$. 2000 units would give $2000 \times 70 = 140000$, not 112000. It would give chiral centres, but the mass rule fails.
